Before turning to causal questions,
it helps to separate them from descriptive ones.

Suppose we want to know how heavy a cow will be
if it eats grass all summer.
This question is a descriptive question about the conditional distribution of weight given diet,
$\p(Y = y \mid X = \text{grass})$,
where $Y$ is weight and $X$ is diet.
We have not asked how heavy a cow would be
if we *intervened* to make it eat grass all summer.

Suppose we find some cows eating grass and others eating hay.
We can observe the weights of the grass-fed cows
and the weights of the hay-fed cows,
but we cannot observe what would have happened
if we had made the grass-fed cows eat hay instead.
Would they have weighed the same as the cows we found eating hay?
Several things could make the answer no:

- the two groups might differ in breed;
- the way the cows ended up with their diets might matter:
  perhaps the bigger cows chased the smaller ones off the grass.

We can answer causal questions of this kind,
but we generally need to answer the descriptive questions first.
Descriptive questions do not require [covariates](Intro-to-GLMs.qmd#def-predictors) that we *could* intervene on;
they only require covariates that we can observe.
This hypothetical example illustrates the distinction
that the [potential outcomes](#def-potential-outcomes) framework of this chapter makes precise.
